overview: Hallenstein Glasson Holdings is a NZX-listed vertically-managed fashion retailer operating two owned brands: Glassons (young women's fashion) and Hallenstein Brothers (menswear), across New Zealand and Australia. The Group designs and sources its own product ranges (manufactured by third-party factories in China, India, Bangladesh and Vietnam) and sells through a network of stores plus growing online channels, rather than owning manufacturing. In FY2026 (year ended 1 August 2026) group sales grew 19.6% to $563.0m, with Net Profit After Tax up 49.9% to $59.2m, as Glassons Australia (now ~58% of group sales) continued to drive growth well ahead of the mature New Zealand market.

business_model.summary: Vertically-managed specialty apparel retail: HGHL designs and buys product ranges directly (not third-party wholesale brands), manages its own supply chain relationships in Asia, and sells through company-operated stores and owned e-commerce sites (glassons.com, hallensteins.com). Revenue is transactional (point-of-sale retail), not recurring/subscription, and highly seasonal (skewed to key trading periods like Black Friday, Christmas and back-to-school/Easter). FY2026 was a breakout year: group sales +19.6%, gross margin expanded 240bps to 61.7%, and NPAT grew nearly 50%, with Glassons Australia now firmly the dominant segment.
business_model.customer_type: B2C - mass-market/value fashion for young women (Glassons) and men (Hallensteins), price points broadly $20-150
business_model.geographic_mix: FY2026: Glassons Australia $324.4m external sales (57.6% of group, +29.0% YoY), Glassons NZ $124.8m (22.2%, +11.5% YoY), Hallensteins (NZ+Australia combined) $113.8m (20.2%, +6.1% YoY); Australia has gone from slightly ahead of NZ to clearly dominant within two years
business_model.online_channel: Digital/e-commerce has been running at roughly 18% of Group revenue and growing faster than store sales as customers shift to an omni-channel model; FY2026 result commentary continued to credit online growth alongside new/refurbished stores for the sales acceleration

competitive_position.market_position: Leading NZ-headquartered specialty apparel retailer by market share in the NZ clothing retailing category; in Australia it has scaled rapidly over the last two to three years and is now a credible mid-tier value/fast-fashion challenger, though still small relative to Cotton On and the department stores in the much larger Australian market

moat_factors.description: In-house design and direct factory sourcing (China, India, Bangladesh, Vietnam) allows faster trend response and margin control versus pure wholesale retailers, though HGHL does not own factories; FY2026 gross margin expansion to 61.7% (+240bps) despite FX evidences continued sourcing/pricing discipline

moat_factors.factor: Brand recognition/heritage in NZ, now scaling in Australia
moat_factors.description: Glassons and Hallensteins are long-established, trusted NZ brands with strong store network density and customer loyalty; two to three consecutive years of double-digit-plus Australian growth (now culminating in FY2026's 29% Glassons Australia growth) suggest the brand is gaining real traction with Australian consumers, not just NZ heritage

Physical stores combined with online create a frictionless browse-in-store/buy-online experience; ongoing store refurbishment and new-store programme (including Burwood NSW) keeps the fleet contemporary and expanding

Net cash position (cash + short-term deposits of $88.2m vs no external bank debt, only IFRS 16 lease liabilities), strong operating cash generation ($122.2m FY2026 operating cash flow) funds store rollout, the new Sydney warehouse and dividends entirely from internally generated cash

Purpose-built automated warehouse completed during FY2026 and operational from the first week of FY2027, materially increasing capacity and automation for the Australian business and removing what had been a logistics constraint on further Australian store growth
Still small relative to global fast-fashion players (Shein, Temu, Cotton On) so lacks their scale-driven sourcing cost advantage

weaknesses: No manufacturing ownership - fully exposed to supplier/factory risk and cannot control landed cost as tightly as vertically-integrated giants
Small scale versus global online-native competitors (Shein, Temu) that can undercut on price with minimal fixed-cost store overhead
Heavy reliance on discretionary consumer spending in only two developed markets (NZ, Australia)

No disclosed hedging programme against USD-denominated inventory purchases - margin is exposed to FX movements each year, though FY2026 showed this can be more than offset by pricing/sourcing management
Recent group CEO churn (two CEOs since 2023, now a decentralised divisional-CEO structure) introduces execution/strategy continuity risk during a critical, now much larger, Australian growth phase

growth_drivers: Glassons Australia scale-up - external sales grew 29.0% to $324.4m in FY2026 (now 58% of group), with the new Burwood NSW store and ongoing refurbishments/relocations (Werribee, Northland Vic, Castle Towers) extending the store network

New automated Sydney distribution centre - completed during FY2026 and operational from the first week of FY2027, adding company-owned automation and capacity to support continued Australian expansion without near-term logistics constraints
E-commerce/digital growth continuing to outpace store sales as omni-channel adoption increases, without major incremental store capex
Hallensteins brand recovery sustained into FY2026 - segment NPAT more than doubled to $7.8m from $3.3m in FY2025, aided by new store concepts and Australian pop-up-to-permanent-store conversions
Store refurbishment and new-store programme across both NZ and Australia lifting like-for-like productivity
Continued gross margin expansion (61.7% FY2026 vs 59.3% FY2025, +240bps) despite ongoing FX headwinds, reflecting sourcing/pricing discipline that has proven durable across multiple years

Strong early FY2027 momentum - first eight weeks of FY2027 trading up 18.4% YoY on a constant-currency basis across both brands, though management cautions this predates the much larger Black Friday/Christmas trading period

business.description: Apparel is highly discretionary; FY2026's strong result followed a period where management had flagged NZ cost-of-living pressures, and the sustainability of double-digit growth into a tougher macro backdrop is unproven
Shein, Temu, ASOS and other online-native players compete aggressively on price with lower overhead, while Cotton On and Kmart contest the value segment directly in both NZ and Australia
Entire business is NZ/Australia apparel retail - no diversification into other geographies or categories, though the Australian growth runway still appears long relative to current scale

Management explicitly cautions that early FY2027 trading (+18.4% constant currency over 8 weeks) 'should not be seen as indicative' of the full year ahead of Black Friday/Christmas, and does not expect the growth rate to be sustained at that level given FY2026's already-strong base

business.risk: CEO/leadership transition and decentralised structure risk
business.description: Group CEO Chris Kinraid resigned September 2025; the Group has since moved to a divisional-CEO model (James McLauchlan at Hallensteins, James Glasson at Glassons Australia) rather than confirming a single group CEO, which could complicate strategic coordination as Australia scales further

financial.description: Product is purchased in USD from Asian factories with no disclosed hedging programme; gross margin is directly exposed to NZD/AUD-USD movements each year - FY2026 again cited FX as a headwind that was more than offset by pricing/sourcing management, but this could reverse in a weaker-currency environment

Lease liabilities grew to $110.6m (current $29.3m + non-current $81.4m) at 1 August 2026, up from $76.6m a year earlier, reflecting the expanding store network and new distribution facility - a larger fixed cost base that pressures margins if sales soften

Capex nearly doubled to $29.4m in FY2026 (from $15.8m) reflecting the Sydney warehouse and store investment; while funded from strong operating cash flow ($122.2m), continued elevated capex needs to keep generating adequate returns

regulatory.description: Changes to de minimis import GST thresholds (as have been debated in Australia/NZ in response to Shein/Temu) could either help (levels playing field) or create compliance complexity
Reliance on third-party factories in China, India, Bangladesh and Vietnam carries ongoing ethical sourcing/labour compliance and reputational risk, actively managed via supplier audits

macro.description: Management's FY2026 outlook again flagged an uncertain economic and geopolitical backdrop, noting consumer spending, FX, freight/logistics and other operating costs could all affect trading and profitability in a manner difficult to predict
New Zealand sales growth (+11.5% FY2026) has been solid but still trails Australia's acceleration (+29.0%), underscoring the Group's growing dependence on the Australian consumer and currency
Global freight rate volatility affects landed cost of imported inventory

macro_factors.industry_outlook: NZ clothing retailing is a mature, low-growth, highly competitive industry; Australian apparel retail is larger and has provided substantial structural growth headroom for Glassons/Hallensteins, now proven out over multiple years of double-digit-plus growth, though the market remains crowded with global fast-fashion and department-store competition
macro_factors.cyclicality: High - apparel is classic consumer discretionary spend, sensitive to real wage growth, interest rates, housing wealth effects, and consumer confidence in both NZ and Australia; FY2026's acceleration came alongside some easing of NZ cost-of-living pressure
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Moderate indirect sensitivity via consumer discretionary spending and mortgage-holder disposable income in NZ/Australia; direct balance-sheet exposure is low given minimal interest-bearing debt outside lease liabilities and a net cash position
macro_factors.currency_exposure: Material - inventory purchased in USD from Asian suppliers with reporting in NZD (consolidated) and AUD (Australian subsidiaries, functional currency changed from NZD to AUD effective FY2025); no disclosed FX hedging programme, so gross margin is directly exposed to USD strength each buying season, though FY2026 showed margin can still expand through pricing/sourcing offsets
key_input_costs: USD-denominated garment/textile costs from China, India, Bangladesh, Vietnam factories

recent_developments.event: Group CEO Chris Kinraid resigned after ~2 years in the role, effective 5 September 2025
James McLauchlan (ex-Kathmandu/KMD Brands CFO) appointed CEO of the Hallensteins brand, reflecting a shift toward a divisional-CEO structure
Annual Meeting trading update: early FY2026 group sales well ahead of prior year, driven primarily by Australia and new/refurbished stores
NZX trading update/profit guidance ahead of half-year results flagging H1 NPBT around $39.8m

H1 FY2026 interim results: sales $275.2m (+14.6%), NPBT $39.8m (+32.9%), gross margin expanded to 60.9% from 58.5%, interim dividend raised to 29.0 cents/share; Sydney automated warehouse construction on track
CEO James McLauchlan increased his personal shareholding via an on-market purchase

FY2026 full-year results (year ended 1 August 2026): Sales Revenue $563.0m (+19.6% vs FY2025's $470.7m); Gross Profit $347.6m (61.7% margin, +240bps); Operating Profit $87.4m; NPAT $59.2m (+49.9%); diluted EPS 99.1 cents. Segment sales: Glassons Australia $324.4m (+29.0%, ~58% of group), Glassons NZ $124.8m (+11.5%), Hallensteins $113.8m (+6.1%)

Final dividend declared at 40.0 cents/share, partially imputed at 91.6% (up from 30.5 cents, 56.5% imputed, a year earlier), payable 9 December 2026; combined with the 29.0 cent interim this takes total FY2026 dividends to 69.0 cents/share, up sharply from FY2025's total of 55.0 cents

New purpose-built, leased Sydney distribution centre with company-owned automation and additional capacity for the Australian business completed during FY2026 and became operational in the first week of FY2027, removing a prior logistics capacity constraint on further Australian store growth

FY2027 early trading update: group sales for the first eight weeks of FY2027 were 18.4% ahead of the prior year on a constant-currency basis, with both Glassons and Hallensteins ahead; management explicitly flagged this is a small part of the year, precedes Black Friday and Christmas, and should not be read as indicative of growth for the rest of H1 FY2027. Next formal trading update due at the December 2026 Annual Meeting

New leased, purpose-built warehouse incorporating company-owned automation and additional capacity for Glassons Australia began operations in the first week of FY2027, supporting continued Australian store growth

guidance.management_commentary: Management highlighted FY2026 as a standout year, with Glassons Australia's continued acceleration (external sales +29.0%) and margin expansion (gross margin +240bps to 61.7%) driving NPAT growth of nearly 50%. The new Sydney distribution centre, completed during the year and operational from the start of FY2027, was framed as removing a capacity constraint ahead of further Australian growth. On FY2027, management reported encouraging early trading (+18.4% constant currency over the first eight weeks) but repeatedly cautioned that this is a small, unrepresentative part of the year ahead of Black Friday and Christmas, and flagged an uncertain economic and geopolitical backdrop -- including consumer spending, FX, freight/logistics and other operating cost risks -- as reasons the Group will 'continue to monitor developments and remain agile' rather than issue formal full-year guidance. A further trading update is due at the December 2026 Annual Meeting.

bull_case: FY2026 proved the Australian growth story at scale - Glassons Australia sales +29.0% to $324.4m (58% of group) with segment NPAT up similarly strongly, and the new automated Sydney warehouse now removes a prior logistics constraint on the next leg of expansion

Gross margin has expanded for multiple consecutive years despite adverse FX (59.3% FY2025 to 61.7% FY2026, +240bps), evidencing durable pricing power and sourcing discipline rather than a one-off tailwind

Strong free cash generation funding a sharply higher dividend (FY2026 total 69.0 cents/share vs 55.0 cents FY2025) from a net-cash balance sheet with no external bank debt, giving a well-covered and growing income stream

Early FY2027 trading (+18.4% constant currency, first 8 weeks) suggests momentum has carried into the new year, with Hallensteins also now contributing meaningfully to growth (segment NPAT more than doubled in FY2026)
Recent insider buying (CEO James McLauchlan's on-market purchase, April 2026) signals management confidence despite the CEO transition
bear_case: FY2026's growth rate (+19.6% sales) sets a materially higher base, and management itself cautions the +18.4% early FY2027 trading pace is unlikely to be sustained once Black Friday/Christmas comparisons bite
No FX hedging disclosed against USD-denominated inventory purchases - a sustained USD rally could compress margins quickly, a risk the company has so far navigated successfully but has not eliminated

Group CEO churn since 2023 and the shift to a decentralised divisional-CEO model raises questions about strategic continuity at a point where the Australian business is now materially larger and more complex (new distribution centre, 40+ stores)

Structurally rising competitive intensity from global online-native fast fashion (Shein, Temu, ASOS) that can undercut on price without store overhead, plus scale disadvantage versus Cotton On and Kmart in the much larger Australian market

Business remains entirely exposed to discretionary apparel spend in just two consumer markets, with capex and lease liabilities both stepping up materially in FY2026 (capex nearly doubled to $29.4m; lease liabilities grew to $110.6m) ahead of proven returns on the expanded footprint
